Field notes on slow software

By Jo Writer, 12 March

Share this essay Tweet Post

Software that takes its time is usually software that someone cared about. This essay collects what we learned from three years of building tools that refuse to hurry, and why we think the pace was the point.

Why speed is a trap

Every team we spoke to measured velocity, and every team we spoke to regretted what the measurement did to their judgement. Fast feels like progress right up until the day you have to understand what you built.

The cost shows up late, in the shape of rewrites and in the quiet loss of people who stopped trusting the codebase. By then nobody remembers which shortcut caused it.

What slowness buys you

Slowness buys review, and review buys shared understanding. A small team that reads each other's work carefully will out-ship a large team that does not, over any horizon longer than a quarter.

  • Write the design note before the code, even when it feels unnecessary.
  • Read every change as if you will maintain it for ten years.
  • Delete more than you add whenever the choice is yours.

What to do on Monday

Pick one habit from the list above and hold it for a month. Resist the urge to adopt all three at once, because the point of going slowly is that you notice what each one changes.
